danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Kort efter klokken ni den aften kørte Weyrother med sine planer til Kutuzovs kvarter, hvor krigsrådet skulle holdes. Alle kolonnekommandørerne var indkaldt til overkommandøren, og med undtagelse af fyrst Bagration, der afslog at komme, var alle til stede på det fastsatte tidspunkt.

Weyrother, der havde fuld kontrol over det planlagte slag, fremviste med sin iver og beslutsomhed en markant kontrast til den utilfredse og døsige Kutuzov, der modvilligt spillede rollen som formand for krigsrådet. Weyrother virkede som en hest, der løber nedad bakke forspændt en tung vogn. Om han trak den, eller den skubbede ham, vidste han ikke, men han styrtede af sted i hovedkulds fart uden tid til at overveje, hvad denne bevægelse måtte føre til. Weyrother havde to gange den aften været ved fjendens forpostkæde for personligt at rekognoscere og to gange hos de to kejsere, den russiske og den østrigske, for at rapportere og forklare, og på sit hovedkvarter, hvor han havde dikteret dispositionerne på tysk, og nu, stærkt udmattet, ankom han til Kutuzovs kvarter.

Han var så åbenbart optaget, at han glemte at være høflig over for overkommandøren. Han afbrød ham, talte hurtigt og utydeligt uden at se på den, han henvendte sig til, og svarede ikke på spørgsmål. Han var tilstænket med mudder og havde et ynkeligt, træt og forvirret udseende, men var samtidig hovmodig og selvtillidende.

Kutuzov havde til huse i et beskedent adeligt landsted nær Ostralitz. I den store salon, der var blevet overkommandørens kontor, var Kutuzov selv, Weyrother og krigsrådets medlemmer samlet. De drak te og ventede kun på fyrst Bagration for at begynde rådslagningen. Endelig kom Bagrations ordonnans med besked om, at fyrsten ikke kunne komme. Fyrst Andrej trådte ind for at meddele overkommandøren dette og forblev, i henhold til den tilladelse Kutuzov tidligere havde givet ham, i værelset.
»Da fyrst Bagration ikke kommer, kan vi begynde,« sagde Weyrother og rejste sig hastigt fra sin plads og gik hen til bordet, hvor et enormt kort over Brünns omegn var bredt ud.

Kutuzov, med uniformen knappet op, så hans fede hals bugnede over kraven som for at slippe fri, sad halvt sovende i en lav stol med sine buttede, gamle hænder hvilende symmetrisk på armlænene. Ved lyden af Weyrothers stemme åbnede han med besvær sit ene øje.
»Ja, ja, hvis De vil være så venlig! Det er allerede sent,« sagde han, nikkede med hovedet, lod det synke og lukkede øjet igen.

Hvis medlemmerne af rådet i begyndelsen troede, at Kutuzov lod som om han sov, beviste de lyde, hans næse udsendte under den efterfølgende oplæsning, at overkommandøren i det øjeblik var optaget af en langt vigtigere sag end ønsket om at vise sin foragt for dispositionerne eller noget andet — han var i færd med at tilfredsstille det uimodståelige menneskelige behov for søvn. Han sov virkelig. Weyrother kastede med den gestus, en mand gør, der er for travl til at spilde et øjeblik, et blik på Kutuzov, og da han havde forvisset sig om, at denne sov, tog han et papir og begyndte med høj, monoton stemme at oplæse dispositionerne for det forestående slag under en overskrift, som han også læste op:
»Dispositioner for et angreb på fjendens stilling bag Kobelnitz og Sokolnitz den 30. november 1805.«
Dispositionerne var meget komplicerede og vanskelige. De begyndte således:

»Da fjendens venstre fløj støtter sig til skovklædte bakker, og hans højre fløj strækker sig langs Kobelnitz og Sokolnitz bag de damme, der findes der, mens vi derimod med vores venstre fløj langt overfløjer hans højre, er det fordelagtigt at angribe fjendens sidstnævnte fløj, især hvis vi besætter landsbyerne Sokolnitz og Kobelnitz, hvorved vi både kan falde ham i flanken og forfølge ham over sletten mellem Schlappanitz og Thuerassa-skoven, idet vi undgår snævringerne ved Schlappanitz og Bellowitz, der dækker fjendens front. I dette øjemed er det nødvendigt, at ... Den første kolonne marcherer ... Den anden kolonne marcherer ... Den tredje kolonne marcherer ...« og så videre, læste Weyrother.

Generalerne syntes at lytte modvilligt til de vanskelige dispositioner. Den høje, lyshårede general Buxhöwden stod lænet med ryggen mod væggen, øjnene fæstet på et brændende lys, og syntes hverken at lytte eller ønske at give indtryk af at lytte. Lige over for Weyrother, med glinsende vidtåbne øjne rettet mod ham og overskægget drejet opad, sad den rødmussede Miloradovitj i en militær positur med albuerne vendt udad, hænderne på knæene og skuldrene hævet. Han forblev hårdnakket tavs og stirrede på Weyrothers ansigt og vendte først blikket bort, da den østrigske stabschef var færdig med at læse. Så så Miloradovitj sig betydningsfuldt om på de andre generaler. Men man kunne ikke af dette blik aflæse, om han var enig eller uenig, tilfreds eller utilfreds med planerne. Ved siden af Weyrother sad grev Langeron, der med et fint smil, som ikke forlod hans typisk sydfranske ansigt under hele oplæsningen, betragtede sine slanke fingre, der hurtigt drejede en gulddåse med et portræt på låget rundt i hjørnerne. Midt i en af de længste sætninger standsede han dåsens drejning, hævede hovedet og ønskede med fjendtlig høflighed lurkende i mundvigene at afbryde Weyrother for at sige noget. Men den østrigske general fortsatte læsningen, rynkede vredt brynene og gik med albuerne, som for at sige: 'I kan komme med jeres synspunkter senere; nu vær så venlig at se på kortet og lytte.' Langeron hævede øjnene med et forvirret udtryk, vendte sig mod Miloradovitj som for at søge en forklaring, men da han mødte dennes imponerende, men intetsigende blik, sænkede han bedrøvet øjnene og tog igen til at dreje sin dåse.
»En geografitime!« mumlede han, tilsyneladende for sig selv, men højt nok til at blive hørt.

Przebyszewski holdt med respektfuld, men værdig høflighed hånden til øret i retning af Weyrother med den mine, en mand har, der er opslugt af at lytte. Dokhturov, en lille mand, sad over for Weyrother med en flittig og beskeden mine, og bøjet over det udbredte kort studerede han samvittighedsfuldt dispositionerne og det ukendte terræn. Han bad Weyrother flere gange gentage ord, han ikke tydeligt havde hørt, og de vanskelige navne på landsbyer. Weyrother efterkom det, og Dokhturov noterede dem.

Da oplæsningen, der varede over en time, var forbi, bragte Langeron igen sin dåse til hvile og begyndte, uden at se på Weyrother eller nogen bestemt, at tale om, hvor vanskeligt det var at gennemføre en sådan plan, hvor fjendens stilling blev antaget som kendt, mens den muligvis ikke var det, da fjenden var i bevægelse. Langerons indvendinger var berettigede, men det var tydeligt, at deres vigtigste formål var at vise general Weyrother — der havde oplæst sine dispositioner med en selvtillid, som var han en lærer, der henvendte sig til skolebørn — at han havde at gøre, ikke med tåber, men med mænd, der kunne lære ham et og andet om krigsførelse.

Da den monotone lyd af Weyrothers stemme ophørte, åbnede Kutuzov sit øje, som en møller vågner op, når møllehjulets søvndyssende summen afbrydes. Han lyttede til, hvad Langeron sagde, som om han bemærkede: 'Er I stadig i gang med det tåbelige?' lukkede hurtigt øjet igen og lod hovedet synke endnu dybere.

Langeron forsøgte så giftigt som muligt at stikke til Weyrothers forfængelighed som ophavsmand til krigsplanen og argumenterede for, at Bonaparte let kunne angribe i stedet for at blive angrebet og dermed gøre hele denne plan fuldstændig værdiløs. Weyrother mødte alle indvendinger med et fast og foragteligt smil, tydeligvis forberedt på forhånd på at imødegå enhver indsigelse, hvad den end måtte være.
»Hvis han kunne angribe os, ville han have gjort det i dag,« sagde han.
»Så De mener, han er magtesløs?« sagde Langeron.
»Han har højst fyrre tusind mand,« svarede Weyrother med det smil, en læge har til en gammel kone, der vil forklare ham, hvordan en sygdom skal behandles.
»I så fald inviterer han sin egen undergang ved at afvente vores angreb,« sagde Langeron med et fint ironisk smil og så sig igen om efter støtte fra Miloradovitj, der var i nærheden.
Men Miloradovitj tænkte i det øjeblik øjensynligt på alt andet end det, generalerne diskuterede.
»Ma foi!« sagde han, »i morgen ser vi det hele på slagmarken.«

Weyrother gav igen det smil, der syntes at sige, at det for ham var mærkeligt og latterligt at møde indvendinger fra russiske generaler og at skulle bevise for dem, hvad han ikke blot selv var overbevist om, men også havde overbevist de to kejsere om.

»Fjenden har slukket sine bål, og der høres en vedvarende støj fra hans lejr,« sagde han. »Hvad betyder det? Enten trækker han sig tilbage — det eneste vi behøver at frygte — eller han skifter position.« Han smilede ironisk. »Men selv om han også indtog en stilling i Thuerassa, sparer han os blot for en masse besvær, og alle vores planer ned til mindste detalje forbliver de samme.«
»Hvordan det ...?« begyndte fyrst Andrej, der længe havde ventet på en lejlighed til at give udtryk for sine tvivl.
Her vågnede Kutuzov, hostede kraftigt og så sig om på generalerne.

»Mine herrer, dispositionerne for i morgen — eller rettere for i dag, for klokken er over tolv — kan ikke nu ændres,« sagde han. »I har hørt dem, og vi skal alle gøre vores pligt. Men før et slag er der intet vigtigere ...« han holdt en pause, »end at sove godt.«
Han bevægede sig, som om han ville rejse sig. Generalerne bukkede og trak sig tilbage. Det var over midnat. Fyrst Andrej gik ud.

Krigsrådet, hvor fyrst Andrej ikke havde fået lejlighed til at give udtryk for sin mening, som han havde håbet, efterlod et vagt og uroligt indtryk på ham. Om det var Dolgorukov og Weyrother eller Kutuzov, Langeron og de andre, der ikke bifaldt angrebsplanen, der havde ret — det vidste han ikke. »Men var det virkelig ikke muligt for Kutuzov at sige sin mening klart til kejseren? Er det muligt, at på grund af hof- og personlige hensyn skal titusinder af liv, og mit liv,« tænkte han, »sættes på spil?«

»Ja, det er meget sandsynligt, at jeg bliver dræbt i morgen,« tænkte han. Og pludselig, ved denne tanke om døden, rejste sig i hans fantasi en hel række af de fjerneste, mest intime minder: han huskede sin sidste afsked med sin far og sin hustru; han huskede de dage, da han først elskede hende. Han tænkte på hendes graviditet og følte medlidenhed med hende og med sig selv, og i en nervøst bevæget og blødgjort stemning gik han ud af det hus, hvor han var indkvarteret hos Nesvitskij, og begyndte at gå frem og tilbage foran det.

Natten var tåget, og gennem tågen skinnede måneskinnet mystisk. »Ja, i morgen, i morgen!« tænkte han. »I morgen kan alt være forbi for mig! Alle disse minder vil ikke mere eksistere, ingen af dem vil have nogen betydning for mig. I morgen måske, ja sikkert, har jeg en forudanelse om, at jeg for første gang må vise alt, hvad jeg kan.« Og hans fantasi malede slaget, dets tab, kampen samlet om ét punkt og alle kommandørernes vaklen. Og så det lykkelige øjeblik, det Toulon, han så længe havde ventet på, melder sig endelig for ham. Han fremlægger fast og klart sin mening for Kutuzov, for Weyrother og for kejserne. Alle er slået af rigtigheden i hans synspunkter, men ingen påtager sig at gennemføre dem, så han tager et regiment, en division — betinger sig, at ingen blander sig i hans dispositioner — fører sin division til det afgørende punkt og vinder sejren alene. »Men døden og lidelsen?« foreslog en anden stemme. Fyrst Andrej svarede imidlertid ikke den stemme og fortsatte med at drømme om sine triumfer. Dispositionerne for det næste slag planlægges af ham alene. Formelt er han kun adjudant ved Kutuzovs stab, men han gør alting alene. Det næste slag vindes af ham alene. Kutuzov fjernes, og han udnævnes... »Nå, og hvad så?« spurgte den anden stemme. »Hvis du inden da ikke er blevet ti gange såret, dræbt eller forrådt — nå, hvad så?...« »Nå, så,« svarede fyrst Andrej sig selv, »ved jeg ikke, hvad der vil ske, og vil ikke vide det og kan ikke; men hvis jeg ønsker dette — ønsker ære, ønsker at være kendt af mennesker, ønsker at blive elsket af dem, er det ikke min skyld, at jeg ønsker det og ikke ønsker andet og kun lever for det. Ja, kun for det! Jeg vil aldrig sige det til nogen, men, oh Gud! Hvad skal jeg gøre, når jeg ikke elsker andet end berømmelse og menneskers anerkendelse? Døden, sår, tabet af min familie — intet frygter jeg. Og kostbare og kære som mange mennesker er for mig — far, søster, hustru — de kæreste jeg har — dog, hvor forfærdeligt og unaturligt det end synes, ville jeg give dem alle på én gang for et øjeblik af ære, af triumf over mennesker, af kærlighed fra mennesker, jeg ikke kender og aldrig vil kende, for kærligheden fra disse mænd her,« tænkte han, mens han lyttede til stemmer i Kutuzovs gård. Stemmerne tilhørte ordonnanserne, der var ved at pakke; én stemme, sandsynligvis en kusks, drillede Kutuzovs gamle kok, som fyrst Andrej kendte, og som hed Tit. Han sagde: »Tit, hør, Tit!«
»Hvad?« svarede den gamle.
»Gå ud, Tit, og tærsk lidt!« sagde spøgefuglen.
»Åh, rend mig i røven!« lød en stemme, der druknede i ordonnansernes og tjenernes latter.
»Alligevel elsker og værdsætter jeg intet andet end triumf over dem alle, jeg værdsætter denne mystiske magt og ære, der svæver her over mig i denne tåge!«

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Shortly after nine that evening, Weyrother arrived at Kutuzov's quarters with his plans for the council of war. All the column commanders had been summoned, and all except Prince Bagration, who declined to attend, were there at the appointed time.

Weyrother, who was fully in charge of the planned battle, presented a sharp contrast in his eagerness and energy to the dissatisfied and drowsy Kutuzov, who reluctantly played the role of chairman. Weyrother was clearly aware he was driving a movement that had already become unstoppable. He was like a horse harnessed to a heavy cart running downhill — whether he was pulling it or being pushed by it, he couldn't tell, but he rushed forward at breakneck speed with no time to think about where this was all heading. He had been to the enemy's picket line twice that evening to scout in person, twice to the Russian and Austrian Emperors to report and explain, and to his own headquarters where he had dictated the battle plan in German. Now, thoroughly exhausted, he arrived at Kutuzov's.

He was so preoccupied that he forgot even basic courtesy toward the commander in chief. He interrupted him, spoke rapidly and indistinctly without looking at the person he was addressing, and ignored questions put to him. He was spattered with mud and had a harried, exhausted, distracted look about him, though at the same time he was arrogant and self-assured.

Kutuzov was occupying a modest nobleman's manor near Ostralitz. In the large drawing room that had become the commander in chief's office, Kutuzov himself, Weyrother, and the other council members had gathered. They were drinking tea and waiting only for Prince Bagration to begin. Finally Bagration's orderly arrived with the news that the prince could not attend. Prince Andrew came in to report this to the commander in chief and, having previously received Kutuzov's permission to attend the council, remained in the room.
"Since Prince Bagration isn't coming, we may as well begin," said Weyrother, hurriedly rising and going to the table where an enormous map of the area around Brunn was spread out.

Kutuzov, his uniform unbuttoned so that his thick neck bulged over his collar as though trying to escape, sat almost asleep in a low chair, his pudgy old hands resting symmetrically on the armrests. At the sound of Weyrother's voice, he opened one eye with effort.
"Yes, yes, go ahead. It's already late," he said, and nodding his head he let it droop and closed his eye again.

If at first the council members thought Kutuzov was only pretending to sleep, the sounds that soon came from his nose proved that the commander in chief was absorbed by something far more pressing than any desire to show his contempt for the battle plan or anything else — he was satisfying the irresistible human need for sleep. He was genuinely asleep. Weyrother, with the manner of a man too busy to waste a single moment, glanced at Kutuzov, confirmed he was asleep, picked up a paper, and in a loud, monotonous voice began reading out the battle plan, starting with its title:
"Dispositions for an attack on the enemy position behind Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz, November 30, 1805."
The dispositions were extremely complicated and difficult to follow. They began:

"Since the enemy's left wing rests on wooded hills and his right extends along Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz behind the ponds there, while we on the other hand far outflank his right with our left wing, it is advantageous to attack the enemy's right wing, especially if we occupy the villages of Sokolnitz and Kobelnitz, whereby we can both strike his flank and pursue him across the plain between Schlappanitz and the Thuerassa forest, avoiding the defiles of Schlappanitz and Bellowitz that cover the enemy's front. To this end it is necessary that... The first column marches... The second column marches... The third column marches..." and so on, Weyrother read.

The generals appeared to listen reluctantly to the complicated orders. The tall, fair-haired General Buxhowden stood leaning against the wall, his eyes fixed on a burning candle, seeming not to listen — or even wanting to be thought to listen. Directly opposite Weyrother sat the ruddy-faced Miloradovich, holding a military pose with his elbows out, hands on his knees, and shoulders raised, his glistening wide eyes fixed on Weyrother and his mustache twisted upward. He remained stubbornly silent, staring at Weyrother's face, and only looked away when the Austrian chief of staff finished reading. Then Miloradovich glanced around meaningfully at the other generals, though it was impossible to tell from that look whether he agreed or disagreed, was satisfied or not. Beside Weyrother sat Count Langeron, who wore the subtle smile that never left his typically southern French face throughout the entire reading, as he gazed at his slender fingers rapidly spinning a gold snuffbox adorned with a portrait. Midway through one of the longest sentences, he stopped spinning the snuffbox, raised his head, and with a thin-lipped smile of hostile politeness tried to interrupt Weyrother to make a point. But the Austrian general, still reading, frowned angrily and jerked his elbows, as if to say: "You can share your views later — for now, kindly look at the map and listen." Langeron raised his eyebrows in confusion, glanced at Miloradovich as if seeking support, but meeting the latter's impressive yet meaningless gaze, he dropped his eyes sadly and went back to spinning his snuffbox.
"A geography lesson!" he muttered, seemingly to himself but loud enough for everyone to hear.

Przhebyshevsky, with respectful but dignified politeness, cupped his hand to his ear toward Weyrother, with the air of a man deeply absorbed in concentration. Dokhturov, a small man sitting opposite Weyrother, leaned over the spread-out map with a conscientious and modest expression, earnestly studying the battle plan and the unfamiliar terrain. He asked Weyrother several times to repeat words he hadn't caught clearly and the difficult names of villages. Weyrother obliged, and Dokhturov noted them down.

When the reading — which lasted more than an hour — was over, Langeron set down his snuffbox again and, without looking at Weyrother or anyone in particular, began explaining how difficult it would be to carry out such a plan when the enemy's position was only assumed and not actually known, since the enemy might well be on the move. Langeron's objections were valid, but it was clear that his main purpose was to show General Weyrother — who had read his plan with the self-assurance of a teacher lecturing schoolchildren — that he was not dealing with fools, but with men who could teach him a thing or two about military affairs.

When the monotonous drone of Weyrother's voice stopped, Kutuzov opened his eye the way a miller wakes up when the soothing hum of the mill wheel suddenly stops. He listened to Langeron's remarks as if to say, "So you're still going on with this nonsense!" then quickly closed his eye again and let his head sink even lower.

Langeron, trying as sharply as possible to wound Weyrother's pride as the plan's author, argued that Bonaparte might easily attack rather than be attacked, which would make the entire plan worthless. Weyrother met every objection with a firm, contemptuous smile, clearly having prepared responses to any possible criticism.
"If he could have attacked us, he would have done so today," he said.
"So you think he's powerless?" said Langeron.
"He has forty thousand men at most," Weyrother replied, with the smile of a doctor whose elderly patient is trying to tell him how to treat the case.
"In that case he's practically inviting his own destruction by waiting for our attack," said Langeron with a subtly mocking smile, again glancing around at Miloradovich for support.
But Miloradovich was obviously thinking about anything other than what the generals were arguing about.
"Well!" he said. "Tomorrow we'll see it all on the battlefield."

Weyrother again gave that smile that seemed to say he found it both strange and absurd to face objections from Russian generals and to have to prove things he had already convinced not just himself of, but the Emperors as well.

"The enemy has put out his fires and there's a constant noise coming from his camp," he said. "What does that mean? Either he's retreating — which is the only thing we need to worry about — or he's changing position." He smiled knowingly. "But even if he also takes up a position in the Thuerassa, he merely saves us a great deal of trouble, and all our plans down to the smallest detail remain the same."
"How is that..." Prince Andrew began. He had been waiting a long time for a chance to voice his doubts.
But at that moment Kutuzov woke up, coughed heavily, and looked around at the generals.

"Gentlemen, the plans for tomorrow — or rather for today, since it is past midnight — can no longer be changed," he said. "You have heard them, and we shall all do our duty. But before a battle, there is nothing more important..." He paused. "...than a good night's sleep."
He moved as if to stand. The generals bowed and withdrew. It was past midnight. Prince Andrew went out.

The council of war, at which Prince Andrew had not managed to express the opinion he'd hoped to share, left him with a vague, uneasy feeling. Whether Dolgorukov and Weyrother were right, or Kutuzov, Langeron, and the others who opposed the plan of attack — he couldn't tell. "But was it really impossible for Kutuzov to speak plainly to the Emperor? Is it possible that because of court politics and personal considerations, tens of thousands of lives — and my life, my life," he thought, "must be put at risk?"

"Yes, it's very likely that I'll be killed tomorrow," he thought. And suddenly, at this thought of death, a whole series of distant, deeply personal memories rose in his mind: he remembered his last farewell to his father and his wife; he remembered the early days when he first loved her. He thought about her pregnancy and felt sorry for her, and for himself, and in this nervously emotional, tender mood he walked out of the cabin where he was quartered with Nesvitsky and began pacing back and forth outside it.

The night was foggy, and through the mist the moonlight shimmered eerily. "Yes, tomorrow, tomorrow!" he thought. "Tomorrow everything may be over for me! All these memories will mean nothing — none of them will matter anymore. Tomorrow perhaps — almost certainly — I have a feeling that for the first time I'll have a chance to show everything I'm capable of." And in his imagination the battle unfolded: the defeat, the fighting concentrated at one crucial point, the hesitation of all the commanders. And then that glorious moment — that Toulon he had waited for so long — finally arrives. He states his views firmly and clearly to Kutuzov, to Weyrother, and to the Emperors. Everyone is struck by the brilliance of his analysis, but no one dares to carry it out, so he takes a regiment, a division — on the condition that no one interferes with his command — leads his division to the decisive point, and wins the victory single-handedly. "But death and suffering?" suggested another voice. Prince Andrew, however, did not answer that voice and continued dreaming of his triumphs. The plans for the next battle are drawn up by him alone. Officially he is still just an adjutant on Kutuzov's staff, but he does everything himself. The next battle is won by him alone. Kutuzov is removed, and he is appointed... "And then what?" asked the other voice. "If before that you're not wounded ten times over, or killed, or betrayed — then what?" "Well then," Prince Andrew answered himself, "I don't know what will happen and don't want to know, and can't know. But if I want this — want glory, want to be known, want to be loved — it's not my fault that I want it and want nothing else and live for nothing else. Yes, for that alone! I will never tell anyone this, but oh God! What am I supposed to do if I love nothing but glory and the esteem of others? Death, wounds, the loss of family — none of it frightens me. And dear as so many people are to me — my father, my sister, my wife — the people closest to me — yet terrible and unnatural as it seems, I would give them all up in an instant for one moment of glory, of triumph, of love from people I don't know and never will know — for the love of these men here," he thought, listening to voices in Kutuzov's courtyard. It was the orderlies packing up; one voice, probably a coachman's, was teasing Kutuzov's old cook, whom Prince Andrew knew — a man called Tit. "Tit, hey, Tit!" he was saying.
"What?" the old man replied.
"Go on, Tit, go thresh a bit!" said the joker.
"Oh, go to hell!" called out a voice, drowned by the laughter of the orderlies and servants.
"All the same, I love and value nothing but victory over them all — this mysterious power and glory that hovers here above me in the mist!"
